newsitem.title: CROATIA: UN extends chaos-hit Serb vote in Croatia elections.
newsitem.headline: UN extends chaos-hit Serb vote in Croatia elections.

text.p: The United Nations announced on Sunday that voting by former rebel Serbs in Croatia's elections would be extended into Monday after technical problems delayed the opening of polling stations.

"Polling areas will be kept open in (the Serb enclave of) Eastern Slavonia until 9 p.m. (1900 GMT). Voting will resume at 10 a.m. tomorrow and run until 7 p.m. This is a firm decision," U.N. spokesman Yuri Chizhik told Reuters.

U.N. administrators of Eastern Slavonia had earlier eased technical conditions for the Serbs to vote to make up time lost after ballot boxes were sent to the wrong places and voter lists were found to be deficient.

Serbs were supposed to vote for regional assemblies to assure minority rights when Eastern Slavonia reverts to Croatian state rule this summer six years after it rebelled against Croatia's secession from Yugoslavia.

Municipal and county councils were being elected in the rest of Croatia in a test for President Franjo Tudjman's nationalist HDZ party, whose popularity has declined despite having led Croatia in a successful 1991 war for independence.

Technical difficulties forced polling stations to open hours late in the Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia and thousands of Serbs who showed up had to go home without voting, embarrassing the region's transitional U.N. administration (UNTAES).
UNTAES announced in mid-afternoon that all adult Serbs with Croatian citizenship papers could now cast ballots in the enclave even if their name was not on registration lists.
"People who came earlier and tried to vote but were unable to do so should come back to cast their vote," said Souren Seraydarian, a deputy UNTAES administrator.

U.S. Ambassador Peter Galbraith, monitoring the elections along with a delegation sent by Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, said the Serb turnout looked very large despite organisational problems and this was encouraging.

"For me the most striking bit is the very large number of people who wanted to vote," he told Reuters. "In this respect, nothing could make me more optimistic that (reintegration of Serbs in Croatia) will work.
"I'm personally very encouraged that the overwhelming majority chose to vote and promote their rights," he said, rather than flee to nearby Serbian-led Yugoslavia.

A good quarter of the enclave's 150,000 Serbs are expected to do so despite Tudjman's guarantees of security for fear of vengeance from soon-to-return Croat refugees over the events of 1991, which included mass executions and expulsions.

The U.N.-supervised vote in Eastern Slavonia was supposed to be a model of efficiency in contrast with chaotic elections run in postwar Bosnia last year by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
But it quickly unravelled with almost half the 171 polling stations opening late, ballot papers going astray and registration lists turning out incomplete.
Reuters reporters in the village of Pacetin saw local Serbs crowding in front of a school from the early morning, only to be told to come later as voting materials had not arrived.
UNTAES spokesman Philip Arnold said the difficulties were mainly technical, dismissing any notion that the snarls were an intentional attempt to obstruct the elections.
"There were some logistical problems. We had mismatched ballot packages, some of which were delivered to wrong places."
Disarray was compounded by late Serb requests for Croatian documents which led to last-minute revisions of voting lists.
Vojislav Stanimirovic, head of the Serb party bloc pitted against Tudjman's HDZ party backed by Croat war refugees, said there were "more irregularities going on than regularities".
But he urged his people to wait "in dignity" for the problems to be eliminated "and not allow any incident".

People possessing Croatian documents were missing from lists, whole streets have not been entered, election materials were not in place and more than 3,500 people left stations after waiting for two hours, a Serb party statement said.
In the rest of the country, balloting proceeded as planned. Tudjman voted in an affluent Zagreb district where he lives.

His conservative nationalist HDZ party was tipped to retain power in smaller and rural municipalities but faced possible defeat in large cities, including the capital Zagreb, to coalitions of centre and left-wing parties.
The HDZ's overwhelming majority in parliament's upper House of Counties was also likely to shrink.
